metaTitle: Ticks in Massachusetts: Types, Lyme Map, Season
metaDescription: Deer ticks live in all 14 Massachusetts counties, and residents had 9,715 Lyme cases in 2023. Tick photos, a county Lyme map, the season and what to do.
h1: Ticks in Massachusetts: Species, County Maps, Lyme Data and Tick Season
dek: Which ticks live in Massachusetts, where Lyme disease is most common county by county, when each tick is active, and what the state advises if one bites you.
excerpt: Deer ticks are established in all 14 Massachusetts counties. Species photos, Lyme rates by county, tick season by month and the state's advice on tick testing.

quickAnswer.lead: **Blacklegged (deer) ticks and dog ticks live throughout Massachusetts, and CDC lists deer ticks as established in all 14 counties.** Massachusetts reported 9,715 Lyme disease cases in 2023, the third most of any state, according to [CDC surveillance data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/surveillance-data-1.html). Lone star ticks have settled on Cape Cod and the islands, and the Asian longhorned tick had been confirmed in four counties by April 2025.
bullets: Relative to population, 2023 Lyme rates were highest in Dukes County (Martha's Vineyard) and Nantucket County, above 1,200 cases per 100,000 residents, and lowest in Suffolk County, which includes Boston.
The state health department counted 8,619 Lyme cases in 2025 and, as of October 2026, a preliminary 5,269 for 2026 through September 30.
Ticks are active year-round: the state sees one peak in tick activity from March or April through August and a second in October and November, and most tick-borne illness occurs June through August.
The state's preliminary count showed 13 Powassan virus cases in 2026 through September, already more than its 12 for all of 2025.
As of October 2026, the state health department does not identify or test ticks, and it warns that a tick's test result, positive or negative, is not definitive evidence of whether you were exposed.

body.text: Which ticks live in Massachusetts?

The state health department names three ticks that bite people in Massachusetts. Blacklegged ticks, also called deer ticks, and dog ticks are found throughout the state, and lone star ticks turn up in some places, according to its [tick-borne disease prevention page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/tick-borne-disease-prevention). A fourth species, the Asian longhorned tick, has been confirmed in four counties and is covered further down.

The blacklegged tick matters most for health. The state says it spreads Lyme disease, babesiosis, anaplasmosis, *Borrelia miyamotoi* infection and Powassan virus, and the [state's Lyme disease fact sheet](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/lyme-disease) adds that one bite can pass on more than one of these germs.

body.alt: An adult female blacklegged tick and a much smaller nymph resting side by side on a person's fingertip, showing how small the nymph stage is
body.caption: An adult female blacklegged (deer) tick, left, and a nymph on a fingertip. The state compares nymphs to a poppy seed and adults to a sesame seed, and calls nymphs the bigger concern because they are so hard to see.
body.credit: CDC/ Division of Vector-Borne Diseases Rickettsial Zoonoses Branch; photo: Lauren Bishop (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Dog ticks are bigger and easier to spot. The state puts an adult at about the size of a watermelon seed and says that, in general, only adults bite people. It links dog ticks to Rocky Mountain spotted fever and some types of tularemia, not to Lyme disease, which it ties to deer ticks. For sizes and markings side by side, see [how to tell the common US ticks apart](/blog/what-do-ticks-look-like).

body.alt: Adult female American dog tick on a blade of grass, reddish-brown with a cream and white mottled shield behind the head and pale-banded legs
body.caption: Adult female American dog tick. The pale, mottled shield behind its head sets it apart from the plain dark shield of an adult deer tick.
body.credit: CDC/DVBID/ Gary O. Maupin; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Where are deer ticks found in Massachusetts?

In every county. [CDC's county surveillance table](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/tick-surveillance-data-sets.html), which runs through December 31, 2025, lists blacklegged ticks as established in all 14 Massachusetts counties, from Berkshire County on the New York line to Barnstable County on Cape Cod. Established means six or more ticks of one life stage, or more than one life stage, were collected in a county within 12 months. To compare other states, see [tick maps and Lyme data for every state](/learn/ticks-by-state).

Backyards count too. The state's prevention page says ticks are most likely found in shady, damp, brushy, wooded or grassy areas, especially tall grass, and that this includes your own backyard. Ticks do not fly or jump; they latch on to people and animals that brush against them.
Which germs have been found in Massachusetts ticks?

CDC's companion table records where each germ has been found in host-seeking blacklegged ticks, meaning ticks out looking for a host rather than feeding on one. It is cumulative, and CDC says a county with no record may simply not have been sampled or tested, so a blank is not proof the germ is absent.

head: Germ
Illness
Massachusetts counties with a record
rows: 6: Berkshire, Franklin, Hampden, Hampshire, Plymouth, Worcester
body.caption: Source: [CDC ArboNET Tick Module](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/tick-surveillance-data-sets.html), pathogen table through December 31, 2025.

body.text: Treat the blanks as possible gaps in sampling rather than proof of low risk. The state's Lyme fact sheet says Lyme disease occurs throughout Massachusetts, yet CDC's table records the Lyme germ in ticks from only 6 of the 14 counties. It also has no Massachusetts record of Powassan virus in host-seeking ticks, even though state residents have been diagnosed with Powassan virus disease every year since 2013.
Is the lone star tick in Massachusetts?

Yes, in a few places, mostly on the Cape and islands. [CDC's lone star tick surveillance](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/lone-star-tick-surveillance.html), which runs through 2025, lists the tick as established in Dukes County, which includes Martha's Vineyard, and reported in Barnstable, Middlesex, Nantucket and Worcester counties. The [state's alpha-gal syndrome fact sheet](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/alpha-gal-syndrome-ags) goes further: it says lone star populations have become established on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.

body.title: Lone star tick status by county, Massachusetts, through 2025
body.caption: Established means six or more lone star ticks of one life stage, or more than one life stage, were collected in the county within 12 months; reported means the tick was recorded there in smaller numbers. CDC's data file notes that the Barnstable and Middlesex records come from a 2014 published compilation and were ticks removed from people, a kind of record CDC no longer uses for this map because the person's travel history may be unknown. No record does not mean no ticks: it can mean no one has sampled there. Once a county is listed as established, it stays established.
body.source: [CDC ArboNET Tick Module (county status through Dec 31, 2025)](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/lone-star-tick-surveillance.html)

body.alt: Adult female lone star tick on a green leaf, reddish-brown with long mouthparts and a single pale spot in the middle of its back
body.caption: Adult female lone star tick, named for the single pale spot on its back. The state says nymphs and adult females bite people most often.
body.credit: CDC/ Dr. Amanda Loftis, Dr. William Nicholson, Dr. Will Reeves, Dr. Chris Paddock; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: The state's prevention page says lone star ticks have not been a significant source of infectious disease in Massachusetts, though they can spread tularemia, ehrlichiosis and STARI. Their saliva can irritate the skin, and redness at a bite is not by itself a sign of infection.

In the United States, alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to meat and other products from mammals, is mainly associated with lone star tick bites. The alpha-gal fact sheet says the syndrome is most common in Massachusetts where lone star ticks have become established, and that allergic reactions usually begin 2 to 10 hours after eating. See [alpha-gal syndrome and the tick bites linked to it](/blog/alpha-gal-syndrome) for symptoms and diagnosis.
Has the Asian longhorned tick reached Massachusetts?

Yes. The [national longhorned tick situation report](https://tickapp.tamu.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/30/2025/05/Longhorned-Tick-SitRep-2025-04-22.pdf) from USDA's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, dated April 22, 2025, lists Massachusetts among the states with confirmed local populations and counts confirmed records in 4 of its 14 counties: Barnstable, Berkshire, Dukes and Nantucket.

The report's first-detection table shows the order. The earliest Massachusetts record is a tick collected from a dog in Barnstable County on July 23, 2018, and identified by DNA testing. Next came a dog in Berkshire County in August 2022, then collections from the environment rather than from an animal: on Nantucket in May 2023, confirmed that June by USDA's National Veterinary Services Laboratories, and in Dukes County in June 2023.

body.alt: Asian longhorned tick nymph and a larger adult female, both plain reddish-brown, resting on a U.S. dime for scale
body.caption: An Asian longhorned tick nymph (left) and adult female (right) on a U.S. dime, which shows how small even the adult is.
body.credit: CDC/ DVBD; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: USDA's report describes an East Asian tick that is a serious livestock pest: it bites aggressively and can build heavy infestations on domestic animals, causing stress, slower growth and severe blood loss. Females can reproduce without a male, so a single fed female can start a population, and the species is a known or suspected carrier of germs behind livestock and human diseases. The state's alpha-gal fact sheet adds that in other countries its bites have been reported to cause alpha-gal syndrome.

If you find an unfamiliar tick, the state's [list of tick identification services](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/tick-identification-and-testing-services) shows where one can be identified for a fee, and its prevention page advises asking a veterinarian how best to protect pets and livestock from ticks. For how to recognize this species, see [the Asian longhorned tick guide](/blog/asian-longhorned-tick).
How much Lyme disease does Massachusetts have?

Massachusetts residents reported 9,715 Lyme disease cases in 2023, according to [CDC's Lyme disease surveillance data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/surveillance-data-1.html). Only New York (22,173) and Pennsylvania (16,671) reported more, and Massachusetts accounted for about 11% of the 89,468 cases reported nationwide. Its rate of 138.9 cases per 100,000 residents ranked fifth, behind Rhode Island, Vermont, Maine and West Virginia.

body.title: Reported Lyme disease cases in Massachusetts, 2008 to 2025
body.yLabel: Cases per year, by place of residence
body.caption: Confirmed and probable cases. CDC's figures run through 2023, its latest year as of October 2026; 2024 and 2025 are the state health department's counts (its 2023 count, 9,728, is close to CDC's 9,715). The near-empty bars for 2016 to 2021 reflect a change in how cases were recorded, not a drop in disease. A revised case definition took effect in 2022, so 2022 onward is not directly comparable with earlier years, and CDC says COVID-19 left 2019 and 2020 data incomplete in some states.
body.source: [CDC Lyme disease surveillance data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/surveillance-data-1.html) through 2023; [Massachusetts Department of Public Health surveillance data](https://www.mass.gov/lists/tick-borne-disease-surveillance-summaries-and-data) for 2024 and 2025

body.text: Read the dip as a counting problem. As Lyme cases grew, collecting clinical information on them became too much work in several high-incidence states, and Massachusetts and New York adopted their own methods that often kept cases from reaching CDC, according to [CDC's report on the revised case definition](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/wr/mm7306a1.htm). The [state's surveillance table](https://www.mass.gov/lists/tick-borne-disease-surveillance-summaries-and-data) spells out the result: from 2016 through 2021, cases were reported without active public health follow-up, so very few patients had enough information on record to count. CDC's Massachusetts totals for those years ranged from 410 down to 7.

Since January 1, 2022, a revised national definition has let high-incidence states such as Massachusetts count cases on laboratory evidence alone, and the state now records them as probable cases. CDC's report says the jump in national case numbers in 2022 likely reflects that change rather than a true increase in risk, and that it limits comparisons with earlier years.

The state's own table carries the count forward: 8,840 cases in 2024 and 8,619 in 2025, both below the 2023 high. As of October 2026 it showed 5,269 cases for 2026 through September 30, a preliminary count that covers only nine months. The state's [monthly tick reports](https://www.mass.gov/lists/monthly-tick-borne-disease-reports) say tick-borne diseases are diagnosed most often in children and older adults.
How does Massachusetts compare with its neighbors?
Lyme disease is common across New England and New York, and two of Massachusetts's neighbors, Rhode Island and Vermont, had the highest rates of any state in 2023.

body.text: Which Massachusetts counties have the most Lyme disease?

Relative to population, the islands. In 2023, Dukes County, which includes Martha's Vineyard, recorded about 1,600 Lyme cases per 100,000 residents and Nantucket County about 1,270, roughly 9 to 12 times the statewide rate. Berkshire County in the far west came third, at about 456. The map shows the 2023 rate for every county, calculated by BuzzSkito from [CDC's county-level Lyme data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/lyme-disease-case-map.html) and the [Census Bureau's county population estimates](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-counties-total.html).

body.title: Lyme disease cases per 100,000 residents by county, Massachusetts, 2023
body.caption: Confirmed and probable cases by county of residence. Rates are BuzzSkito's calculation: CDC's 2023 county counts divided by the Census Bureau's July 1, 2023 population estimates (Vintage 2025). CDC's county file places 9,682 of the state's 9,715 cases in a county; calculated this way, the statewide rate is 136.9, close to CDC's 138.9. Small counties swing sharply: Nantucket's 185 cases came from about 14,600 residents.
body.source: [CDC county-level Lyme disease data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/lyme-disease-case-map.html), 2023; [U.S. Census Bureau county population estimates](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-counties-total.html)

head: County
Lyme cases, 2023
Cases per 100,000
body.caption: All 14 counties, highest rate first. Sources as for the map.

body.text: Raw counts follow population instead. Bristol County had the most cases in 2023 (1,688), followed by Plymouth (1,385) and Middlesex (1,348). Middlesex is the most populous county in the state, and its rate of 82 per 100,000 was well below the statewide figure. Suffolk County, which includes Boston, had the lowest rate, 29.2.

Two cautions apply to any county figure. Cases are counted where the patient lives, not necessarily where the bite happened, as [CDC's Lyme case map page](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/lyme-disease-case-map.html) notes, so a Boston resident bitten on Cape Cod is counted in Suffolk County and summer visitors to the islands are counted at home. And island rates move fast: with about 21,000 residents in Dukes County, each extra case adds almost 5 per 100,000.
Which other tick-borne diseases occur in Massachusetts?

Anaplasmosis and babesiosis come next, and both are spread by the same blacklegged tick. The [state's surveillance table](https://www.mass.gov/lists/tick-borne-disease-surveillance-summaries-and-data) counted 1,496 anaplasmosis cases and 881 babesiosis cases in 2025, the most for each in any year since the table begins in 2015. It also counted 107 cases of *Borrelia miyamotoi* infection in 2025, another high for the table.

body.text: The state's prevention page also lists tularemia and Rocky Mountain spotted fever among the diseases ticks spread in Massachusetts, and links both to dog ticks. The alpha-gal fact sheet says tularemia occurs on both Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket, and that most of the other infections lone star ticks can carry, such as ehrlichiosis and Heartland virus, are very rare in the state. For symptoms and treatment, see the guides to [anaplasmosis](/blog/anaplasmosis) and [babesiosis](/blog/babesiosis).
How common is Powassan virus in Massachusetts?

It went from no reported cases to about a dozen a year. [CDC's Powassan virus data](https://www.cdc.gov/powassan/data-maps/historic-data.html), which start in 2004, show no Massachusetts cases before 2013 and 83 from 2013 through 2025, including 12 in 2025. Over the whole period only Minnesota and Wisconsin reported more. The state's preliminary count for 2026 had already reached 13 by September 30.

body.title: Powassan virus disease cases in Massachusetts residents, 2008 to 2025
body.yLabel: Cases per year, by county of residence
body.caption: 80 of the 83 cases were the more severe neuroinvasive form, which CDC says is less likely to go unreported than mild illness. The state's [Powassan fact sheet](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/powassan-virus) counts 84 cases for 2013 to 2025; its [surveillance table](https://www.mass.gov/lists/tick-borne-disease-surveillance-summaries-and-data) shows 7 in 2018, where CDC's file shows 6. Data through 2025, finalized September 16, 2026.

body.text: Powassan is rare but serious. The [state's Powassan virus fact sheet](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/powassan-virus) says most people exposed to the virus likely never feel ill, but others develop meningitis or encephalitis; about 10% of people with that severe form die, and there is no specific treatment. It also says there is evidence the virus can pass from a tick in as little as 15 minutes after it attaches. The [Powassan virus guide](/blog/powassan-virus) covers symptoms in more detail.
When is tick season in Massachusetts?

All year, with the most risk from spring through fall. The state's [monthly tick reports](https://www.mass.gov/lists/monthly-tick-borne-disease-reports), which track reported tick bites and tick-borne disease diagnoses, say tick activity and tick-borne diseases occur year-round in Massachusetts. Activity depends on the weather but has two peaks: the first begins in March or April and lasts through August, and the second comes in October and November. Most tick-borne disease cases occur from June through August.

body.caption: A blacklegged tick adult and two much smaller immature ticks. The state says nymphs are most active from May through July, and adults in spring and fall.
body.credit: CDC/ Michael L. Levin, Ph. D. (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Winter is not tick-free. The state's Lyme fact sheet says adult deer ticks may be out looking for a host any time temperatures are above freezing, so a mild winter day in the woods still calls for a tick check. For how the season differs in other parts of the country, see [when tick season starts and ends in each US region](/blog/tick-season).
Can you get a tick identified or tested in Massachusetts?

Yes, but not from the state. As of October 2026, the [state health department's tick testing page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/tick-identification-and-testing-services) says it does not offer tick identification or tick testing. The page lists six labs that identify or test ticks for a fee, three of them in Massachusetts (in Acton, Amherst and Newton), without endorsing any of them. The list was current as of June 2021, so check the details with a lab before sending anything.
The department is cautious about what a result means:

items: **A tick result is not proof either way.** A positive or negative result from a tick that bit you does not show for certain whether you were exposed.
**The tick you found may not be the one.** Most people diagnosed with a tick-borne disease never knew they were bitten, and other ticks may have bitten you too.
**Negative results can mislead.** Lab tests on ticks can, though probably rarely, give false results and may not cover every germ, so keep watching for a rash or fever.
**Do not wait for a result.** Symptoms can start before results arrive, so see a health care provider if you feel sick.
**A positive tick does not automatically mean treatment.** Discuss it with a provider, who will weigh when the bite happened, your symptoms and your likely exposure.

body.text: Tick testing does help track risk across the state. The department notes that the University of Massachusetts Laboratory of Medical Zoology publishes its results free of charge in the Tick-Borne Disease Network passive surveillance database, which shows where infected ticks were found while keeping senders' names and addresses private.
What should you do after a tick bite in Massachusetts?

Remove the tick right away, note the date, and tell a health care provider if it was a deer tick or if you feel ill. The state's [prevention page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/tick-borne-disease-prevention) and Lyme fact sheet describe removal this way:

items: Grip the tick with fine-point tweezers as close to the skin as possible.
Pull straight out with steady pressure, without squeezing or twisting the tick's body.
Skip kerosene, petroleum jelly, nail polish and a hot match tip; the state says they do not work and may cause injury.
Circle the date on a calendar and note where on the body the tick was attached. You may want to save the tick for identification.

body.text: A fuller walk-through is in [the step-by-step tick removal guide](/blog/how-to-remove-tick-safely), and [a full-body tick check](/blog/how-to-do-a-tick-check) shows where ticks hide.

Speed matters. The [state's Lyme disease fact sheet](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/lyme-disease) says a deer tick usually must be attached for at least 24 hours before it can spread the Lyme germ, while its Powassan fact sheet says that virus may pass in as little as 15 minutes. The prevention page adds that a physician may choose to treat you after a deer tick bite, so let your provider know if one bit you.

Then watch for symptoms. Early Lyme disease usually begins 3 to 30 days after the bite. [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/signs-symptoms/index.html) says about 70% to 80% of infected people get a rash called erythema migrans where the tick was attached; it expands over several days, up to 12 inches or more across, and only sometimes clears in the center. Fever, chills, headache, fatigue, muscle and joint aches and swollen lymph nodes can come with it, or without a rash. Untreated, Lyme disease can affect the joints, nerves and heart, and the state's fact sheet says about 60% of untreated people develop arthritis. [The stages of Lyme disease symptoms](/blog/lyme-disease-symptoms-guide) covers what each stage looks like.

body.alt: Expanding red rash with a darker red center and a paler outer ring on the back of a person's upper arm, the erythema migrans rash of early Lyme disease
body.caption: Erythema migrans, the expanding rash of early Lyme disease, here in a bull's-eye pattern. The state notes it does not always clear in the center.
body.credit: CDC/ James Gathany; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Alpha-gal syndrome gives a different warning. The state says to talk to a doctor about nausea, vomiting or diarrhea, or signs of an allergic reaction such as face or tongue swelling or hives, within several hours after eating meat or dairy products.

body.title: See a health care provider if you feel ill
body.text: A rash, fever, headache, fatigue or aching muscles in the weeks after a tick bite or time outdoors is a reason to see a provider and mention the tick. Do not wait for a tick test result. This page summarizes what public health agencies publish and is not a diagnosis.
How do you prevent tick bites in Massachusetts?
Use repellent, cover up, stay on the trail and check for ticks every day. The state's Lyme disease fact sheet and prevention page recommend these steps:

items: **Use an EPA-registered repellent.** DEET products can go on skin; the state's Lyme fact sheet says not to use them on children younger than 2 months and to use concentrations of 30% or less on older children. Picaridin, oil of lemon eucalyptus and IR3535 also protect against ticks. Follow the product label.
**Treat clothing, not skin, with permethrin.** The state names clothing, shoes, bed nets and camping gear, and says permethrin should not be applied to skin.
**Cover up and stay central.** Wear a long-sleeved shirt and long, light-colored pants tucked into socks or boots, and keep to the middle of trails, away from the edges where ticks are likely to be.

**Check once a day.** Look over yourself, your children and your pets, especially between the toes, behind the knees, in the groin and armpits, along the hairline, at the back of the neck and behind the ears. Ticks are tiny, so look for new freckles.
**Protect pets.** Ask a veterinarian about tick collars, repellents and other options for dogs and cats; [the guide to ticks on dogs](/blog/ticks-on-dogs) shows where to check a dog.

faqs.question: Are ticks active in Massachusetts in the winter?
faqs.answer: Yes, adult deer ticks can be. The Massachusetts Department of Public Health says adult blacklegged ticks may be out looking for a host any time temperatures are above freezing, and its monthly reports say tick activity and tick-borne diseases occur year-round in the state. Activity peaks from March or April through August and again in October and November, so check for ticks after time in woods, brush or tall grass, even on a mild winter day.

faqs.question: Where in Massachusetts is Lyme disease most common?
faqs.answer: Relative to population, on the islands. In 2023, Dukes County, which includes Martha's Vineyard, had about 1,600 cases per 100,000 residents and Nantucket about 1,270, based on CDC county counts and Census population estimates. Berkshire and Barnstable counties came next. Bristol County had the most cases, 1,688. Cases are counted where patients live, not where they were bitten, and small island populations make rates swing widely.

faqs.question: Does Massachusetts test ticks for Lyme disease?
faqs.answer: No. As of October 2026, the Massachusetts Department of Public Health does not offer tick identification or testing, though it lists labs that offer identification, testing or both for a fee. The department cautions that a positive or negative result from a tick does not prove whether you were infected, and that symptoms can begin before results arrive. If you feel ill after a bite, see a health care provider rather than waiting for a test.

faqs.question: Are lone star ticks in Massachusetts?
faqs.answer: Yes, in a few places. CDC's surveillance lists them as established in Dukes County, which includes Martha's Vineyard, and reported in four other counties, and the state health department says populations have become established on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket. The state says lone star ticks have not been a significant source of infectious disease in Massachusetts, but their bites are linked to alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to meat from mammals.

faqs.question: How long does a tick have to be attached to spread Lyme disease?
faqs.answer: Usually at least 24 hours, according to the Massachusetts Department of Public Health, which is why prompt removal and a daily tick check help. Powassan virus is different: the state says there is evidence it can pass from a tick in as little as 15 minutes. Remove any attached tick right away with fine-point tweezers, note the date, and tell a health care provider if it was a deer tick.

faqs.question: Why did Lyme disease cases in Massachusetts drop after 2015?
faqs.answer: They did not really drop. From 2016 through 2021, Massachusetts recorded cases without the active public health follow-up needed to collect clinical details, so very few patients could be counted, and CDC's totals fell as low as 7 in 2019. Since 2022, a revised case definition has let the state count cases from laboratory evidence alone, and reported cases returned to 5,052 in 2022 and 9,715 in 2023.
